items.e: **When the non-Jew is not in the house, he does not prevent [the eruv]. And it contains one paragraph. **A non-Jew who lives with two Jews, when the non-Jew is not in his home, does not prohibit (see above, siman 371), and they may make an eruv and be permitted. If the non-Jew comes on Shabbat, he prohibits and the eruv is nullified. However, they can rent from him on Shabbat, and afterwards one can nullify his domain to the other, and the individual will be permitted. And all the more so, if the non-Jew died on Shabbat, one can nullify his domain to the other and the individual will be permitted.

**A Non-Jewish Guest, Whether He Prevents [Carrying]. Containing 2 paragraphs:** A non-Jew who enters as a guest: if he entered without permission, he never prevents [carrying]. If he entered with permission — if he regularly comes, he prevents [carrying] immediately. If he does not regularly come, he does not prevent [carrying] until after thirty days.

The king's soldiers who entered into the homes of Jews, whether by force or willingly — if the homeowners have in those places where the non-Jews entered utensils that are forbidden to move on Shabbat, [the non-Jews] do not prevent [carrying] upon them.

**Laws of Sadducee and apostates in eruv. Containing 4 paragraphs. **A Sadducee is like a Jew and can nullify his domain, but an eruv is not effective since he does not acknowledge the validity of eruv.
A Samaritan is like other non-Jews, and has no remedy except through rental [of his domain].

A Jew who has apostatized to idolatry, or who desecrates the Sabbath publicly — even if he violates only a rabbinic prohibition — is like a non-Jew. But if he violates only in private, even a Torah prohibition, he is like a Jew and can nullify his domain.

A Jew who converted [to another religion] and had houses in a Jewish courtyard that made an eruv for the entire year: if he has no other entrance at all, he prohibits [carrying] on every Sabbath that occurs after his conversion. But if he has another entrance to a non-Jewish courtyard — even a small opening that he did not initially use regularly — we push him toward the entrance that opens to the non-Jewish courtyard.

**Laws of partnership in an eruv. Containing 9 paragraphs** The Sages forbade carrying from courtyards into an alleyway, and permitted it through a partnership whereby bread or any other food is collected from each courtyard and placed in one of the courtyards, and we consider it as if the entire alleyway opens into that courtyard. Since this is only to create partnership among the courtyards, it may be placed in the airspace of the courtyard or in a house that is not four by four handbreadths, and need not be placed in a house — only in a protected place. Therefore it may not be placed in the airspace of the alleyway.

Jews living in three separate locations whose gates are each locked at night, and a beadle who collects flour from all of them — this does not help them make a partnership, since an alleyway partnership must be placed in a courtyard within the alleyway, and since they are separate from one another and distant, their partnership is not one and their alleyways are not one. Rema: If they made an eruv in one place, the others who did not make an eruv do not restrict them, since they have no foot traffic over one another, as the entire city is not considered one alleyway even though they live within one surrounding wall.

All the laws of eruv for courtyards — its required amount, that a man's wife may make the eruv on his behalf, that one may make an eruv without someone's knowledge if their house opens only to one courtyard, that a minor may collect it, and that one person may acquire on behalf of all (and that if they were already partners they need not make an eruv) — all these laws apply equally to the partnership eruv. Rema: Even if one was already partnered with his neighbors in merchandise — one in wine and one in oil — they need not make a partnership eruv, provided it is in one vessel.
One may make a partnership eruv with any type of food, and even four or five types of food may combine to make up two meals' worth.

One may make a partnership eruv with any type of food except for berries that have hardened to seed, spices, dry beans, onion tops that have not grown a handbreadth in length, truffles and mushrooms, unripe dates, lentils, wheat and barley, vegetables that are half-cooked, water alone, or salt alone. But if water and salt are mixed together one may use them, and some say only when oil was added to them. Some say one may make an eruv with spices.

For anything normally used as a relish with bread, the required amount is enough to serve as relish for bread eaten at two meals. For anything not used as a relish, the required amount is enough to eat at two meals. Raw meat is not considered a relish and requires enough to eat at two meals. Roasted meat is considered a relish and requires enough to serve as relish for two meals. Vinegar is considered a relish, as is cooked wine, but uncooked wine is not considered a relish and its required amount is two reviit, and similarly for other liquids.

One may make a partnership eruv with two eggs even raw, with two pomegranates, with five peaches, with a litra of vegetables whether raw or cooked, with a handful of fresh beans, or with a kav of forest apples.

One may make a partnership eruv even with food that is not suitable for him, if it is suitable for some person — such as wine for a nazirite or terumah for a Jew. Similarly, one who vowed or swore not to eat something may still make a partnership eruv with it. Some say this applies only when he vowed or swore not to eat it, but if he vowed or swore not to benefit from it, one may not make a partnership eruv with it for him. (And if he said konام on benefiting from it or eating it — according to all opinions one may not make a partnership eruv with it.) (Tur)

If one said of a loaf "today it is unconsecrated and tomorrow it is consecrated" or "konام" — one may make a partnership eruv with it, since during twilight it had not yet certainly become consecrated and it was suitable while it was still day. But if one said "today it is konام and tomorrow it is unconsecrated" — one may not make a partnership eruv with it since it is not suitable until nightfall. A courtyard opening into two alleyways that made a partnership with each of them — it is permitted to carry between it and each of them, but it is forbidden to carry vessels that rested in one alleyway to the other alleyway through the courtyard. If it made no partnership with either of them: if it regularly uses both by entering and exiting through them on weekdays, it restricts both. If it regularly uses one and not the other, the one it regularly uses restricts while the one it does not regularly use does not restrict. If it made a partnership with the one it does not regularly use, the one it regularly uses becomes permitted on its own if they made a partnership among themselves. Similarly, if it regularly uses both and made a partnership with one of them, the other is permitted since it removed itself from it. If the alleyway it regularly uses made a partnership among themselves and the one it does not regularly use did not make a partnership, and it made no partnership with either — we push it toward the one it does not regularly use and it removes itself from the one it regularly uses so that the latter is permitted, since it loses nothing by this as it made no partnership with them, and others gain from it — we compel it on account of the trait of Sodom.

**Partners in an alley must make an eruv in the courtyards. containing 1 paragraph:** Those who partner in an alley must make an eruv in their courtyards, so that children will not forget the law of eruv—since children are not aware of what is done in the alley. Therefore, if they partnered in the alley with bread, one may rely on it and they need not make an eruv in the courtyards, since children recognize bread. Some say that if each courtyard did not make an eruv for itself, one may not rely on the partnership. However, when each courtyard made an eruv for itself and afterward they partnered in the alley but did not make an eruv through the openings between them, they are permitted to use the courtyards in the alley through the openings between them, for one may rely on the partnership in place of an eruv. And if they made an eruv through the openings between them but did not partner in the alley, the courtyards are permitted to use the alley, for one may rely on the eruv that the courtyards made through the openings in place of partnership. Rama: Some say one may rely on partnership in place of eruv even if they only partnered with wine, and similarly one may rely on eruv in place of partnership. Above in siman 366 section 6 I wrote that our practice is initially to make only one partnership with flour. The reason is that our eruv, where each resident of the courtyard contributes to the partnership, constitutes both eruv and partnership together, and initially one should not do more. The requirement for both partnership and eruv was in Talmudic times, when courtyard residents did not contribute to the partnership; rather, the courtyard made an eruv together and one member contributed to the partnership. But in such a case everyone agrees that one only makes one partnership, and if one does more and recites a blessing on it, it is a blessing in vain.

**The law if the courtyards did not establish an eruv together and also did not partner in the alleyway. Containing 1 section.** If the courtyards did not make an eruv together and also did not make a partnership in the alleyway, it is permitted to carry throughout the entire alleyway items that rested in it on Shabbat—whether the courtyards made an eruv with the houses or they did not make an eruv. According to our teacher Rabbi Moshe bar Maimon, this applies specifically when they did not make an eruv of courtyards with the houses. But if they made an eruv of courtyards with the houses, one may only carry in the alleyway within four cubits.

**A Non-Jew who has a window opening to an alleyway. Containing 1 paragraph.** A non-Jew who lives in an alleyway and has a back window of his house opening to a field or yard—even if it is only four by four handbreadths—does not prohibit the residents of the alleyway [from carrying], even if he brings in and takes out camels and wagons through the alleyway all day long. For he prefers the opening in back that is open to him alone, which has air, and his opening to the alleyway is as if he does not regularly use it, so he does not prohibit. This applies when the field or yard is more than two se'ah in area. But if it is only two se'ah, it is small and he is not satisfied with it. A Jew who has an opening to an alleyway and a back opening to a yard, and he forgot and did not make an eruv: if the yard is more than two se'ah, he prohibits, since it is not suitable for him and he does not withdraw from the alleyway. But if it was enclosed for dwelling, even if it is more than two se'ah, he does not prohibit, since it is suitable for him. And there are those who say that on the contrary: if it was enclosed for dwelling, even if it is two se'ah, he prohibits, since when it is enclosed for dwelling it has no air and he does not want to withdraw from the alleyway on its account.

**An alleyway where one side is a non-Jews and one side is a Jews. Containing 2 paragraphs. ** An alleyway where one side is owned by a non-Jew and one side by a Jew, and another Jewish house adjacent opens to the public domain but not to the alleyway, and there is a window between him and the Jew living in the alleyway—[the one whose house opens to the public domain] cannot make an eruv through the window between them to carry his utensils into the alleyway via his Jewish neighbor's house which opens to the alleyway. But if there is a doorway between them, it is permitted. And there is one who prohibits even when there is a doorway open between them.

An alleyway where one side is owned by a non-Jew and one side by Jews, and there were windows open from his courtyard to the Jewish courtyard, and they all made an eruv through the windows—even though they became like members of one household and are permitted to carry in and out through the windows, they are prohibited from using the alleyway through their doorways until they rent [the domain] from the non-Jew.

**Laws of nullifying permission for those who forgot to make an eruv. Containing 2 paragraphs:** Just as the laws of nullification apply to one who forgot and did not establish an eruv in his courtyard, so too in an alleyway — if one courtyard forgot and did not join in the shituf, it may nullify its domain to the other residents of the alleyway, or they may nullify theirs to it, even though they are many. For the residents of a courtyard are considered as a single individual with respect to the alleyway. And just as the laws governing Jews dwelling in a courtyard with non-Jews apply, so too in an alleyway or in a walled city. Carrying is not prohibited in an alleyway or walled city unless there are two courtyards of Jewish homes in the city. But one courtyard alone does not suffice, even if many Jewish homes open into it. This applies when the city is surrounded by a wall built for dwelling. Typical towns are walled for dwelling; typical fortresses are not walled for dwelling. When there are two courtyards of Jewish homes in the city, one must rent from each and every courtyard of non-Jews; it does not suffice to rent from the city official. >Rama: Some say this is only regarding bringing items in and out of the non-Jewish domain, but for carrying in the alleyway, one may rent from the official, since the alleyway belongs to the official and he can remove all the non-Jews from there. This applies to an official who does not own the houses and has no right to use the residents' homes, even in wartime. But where all the city's affairs are conducted only by the official or his appointee, renting from that official or his agent suffices, for he has the right to place his men and weapons in the residents' homes in wartime without their consent.

Jews dwelling alone in a courtyard in a non-Jewish walled city, when other Jews pass through on Shabbat and lodge in a different courtyard, do not prohibit them, for a guest does not prohibit. They are permitted to carry throughout the entire city. (See later Siman 370)

**Laws of City Eruvin. Containing 8 paragraphs:** A city that has been the property of an individual, even if it became public- everyone can join in one partnership, and carry throughout the whole estate. Similarly, if it is publicly owned and it has one entrance- everyone can join in one partnership. But if it is publicly owned and and has two entrances, where the populace goes in one and out the other, even if the area came under private ownership, we may not make the whole thing into an Eruv. Rather, we must exclude a place, even as small as one courtyard and the house within it, from the city, and join the rest of the city together. Then all the participants in the partnership will be permitted in the whole city, except that one place that they excluded, and those residents remaining will be permitted in their own location, through a partnership they make for themselves. But if there are many residents remaining, it is forbidden to carry in the entire city. This is a provision instituted for the purpose of recognition, so that the residents will be aware that the Eruv has permitted them to carry in this place. The public becomes become expert on it, observing that we do not carry in the place that was excluded and not joined with them, but rather these carry in their own space and those carry in their own space. If residents wanted to institute an Eruv for each alley on its own, that would certainly be effective, for there is no greater exclusion than this.

A city of many people that has a first entrance and a ladder in another place, they are all mixed up and it is not necessary to remember that the ladder in the wall is not considered as a door, and even if many ladders are placed side by side up to a width of ten, it is not considered as a door. And if it has two doors and there is a garbage pile in front of one of them, it is as if there is only a first door there:

The houses that are placed separately, even though they are not open to the city, but have their backs to the city and their faces are outside, and even if it is (just one house, even) a cattle house or a hay house that does not need to be fenced, they are considered separate, and the rest of the houses are fenced:

A city in which all its inhabitants participated except one alleyway, then carrying is forbidden to all of them. And if they built a monument at the entrance of the alleyway then carrying is not forbidden to them. Therefore, a city that was the property of a single person, even if it became the property of many, is not divided into halves, but either the whole or both entrances and exits. And each entrance and exit builds a monument at its entrance if he wants to share his permission with them so that he does not prohibit the rest of his entrances.

What is the meaning of the words, "It is not to be built for the half of a city"? That is it is surrounded by a high wall, and it has a gate. But if the whole city were not prepared on the outside, and they came to prepare the half and to build the half, they allowed it in their hands:

The one who qualifies all the inhabitants of the city for participation, if they all participated he does not need to inform them that the right is theirs. And the law for anyone who forgot and did not participate with the inhabitants of the city, or for anyone who went to exile in another city, or for a foreigner who was with them in the city, is the same as the law for the courtyard and in the alleyway:

One does not make eruv chatzeirot (courtyard eruv) or shitufei mevoot (alleyway partnership) on a festival that falls on Friday. But if one forgot and did not make an eruv before the festival, and two festival days fall on Thursday and Friday, one may make an eruv on the festival conditionally, saying: "If today is a weekday, let this be an eruv; if today is holy, my words are nothing." And the next day one says: "If today is holy, I already made an eruv yesterday; if today is a weekday, let this be an eruv." This applies to the two festival days observed in the diaspora, but not to the two days of Rosh Hashanah, for they are considered like one long day. (See below, section 528.)

Both eruv chatzeirot and shitufei mevoot may be established during twilight, even if one has already accepted the addition to Shabbat. Some authorities forbid this if one has already accepted the addition to Shabbat.

If one made an eruv for two people—for one person while it was still day and that eruv was consumed during twilight, and for another person during twilight—both have acquired their eruv. For the one whose eruv was consumed during twilight, we consider it night; for the one whose eruv was placed during twilight, we consider it day. However, if one made an eruv during twilight and it was consumed during twilight, it is forbidden.

*Law regarding a doubtful erev. Containing 3 paragraphs.* A case of doubt regarding an eruv, for example, if there is doubt whether it existed during twilight or not, is permitted, provided it had a presumption of validity. This means it was placed there and then doubt arose about it. However, if there was no presumption of validity, for example, if there is doubt whether it was placed there at all, it is not permitted.

The eruv must be in a place where it is possible to retrieve it during twilight. Therefore, if debris fell upon it and one cannot retrieve it without great effort and tools, it is forbidden. Rema: The eruv need only remain intact during twilight, and may be eaten once it is certainly dark. One should recite a blessing over it on Shabbat morning, but specifically in a place where the practice is to make an eruv every Friday. However, it is even better to make an eruv for the entire year at once, as discussed above in section 368.

If one placed the eruv in a tower and locked it, and the key was lost before nightfall, if it is impossible to remove the eruv unless one performs a complete forbidden labor during twilight, this is equivalent to the eruv being lost, and it is not valid, since it is impossible to eat it.

**Laws of the blessing over an eruv. Contains 1 section** It is a mitzva to take care to arrange partnership of alleyways, and one recites the blessing "on the mitzva of eruv" and says "through this partnership all the residents of the alleyway shall be permitted to carry in and out between the courtyards and the alleyway (and from them to the houses) (Beit Yosef in the name of the Shebolei Leket) on Shabbat." When does one recite the blessing? At the time he collects it from the alleyway residents or at the time he transfers ownership to them. Rema: If they collected it for the purpose of the eruv and forgot and did not recite the blessing over it, it is a valid eruv since the blessing does not invalidate it. (Agur and Shibbolei Haleket) See Siman 366.

"Each man has under him" (_Exodus 16:29_), from this phrase we learn that each person has four amot (cubits) in every place, even if he went outside of the barrier and we measure for each person his "amah", and if he has short limbs, we give him four average-length amot, each of which is six handbreaths. Rema: And these four amot are measured wide with him in the center (Tur). And there are those who say that he is permitted to walk four amot on each side but carrying, he only has four amot at the diagonal, as was explained before in Siman 349 (Tur in the name of the Raza''h and the Maggid Ch. 12 in the name of the Rashbah.)

In any place that he finds himself when Shabbat begins, if he is in an enclosed space for dwelling, even if there are no inhabitants, all of it is considered like four amot, and if it is not an enclosed space for dwelling, until it contains two seahs, all of it is considered like four amot, and even he is on a tall hill, an harvested area with stalks and barley surrounding it, it is considered like four amot until it contains two seahs.

**Laws of an individual's Shabbat rest, his vessels, and traveling two thousand cubits. Contains 18 sections** Every person has two thousand cubits in each direction beyond his four cubits or beyond the place where he spent Shabbat.
If Shabbat came upon him in an open valley and he does not know the Shabbat boundary, he may walk two thousand steps (of average size) (Tur) which constitute the Shabbat boundary.

Just as a person may not walk on Shabbat and Yom Tov more than two thousand cubits in each direction, so too his vessels and animals — no person may take them beyond the two thousand cubits of their owner. If the owner made an eruv in one direction, no person may take them in the other direction even one step to a place where the owner cannot go. Rema: See above at the end of Siman 305 regarding whether one may hand over an animal to a non-Jew in a place where there is concern he may take it beyond the boundary.
One who handed over his animal to his son — it follows the father's boundary.

If he handed it to a shepherd — even if he gave it to him on Yom Tov — it follows the shepherd's boundary. If he handed it to two shepherds, it follows the owner's boundary since neither one acquired it.

An ox designated for slaughter follows the boundary of whoever purchased it to slaughter on Yom Tov. Similarly, if the owner slaughtered it on Yom Tov and sold the meat, each buyer may take his portion wherever he goes.
A shepherd's ox follows the boundary of the people of that town.
Vessels designated for one of the brothers in a household follow his boundary, and those not designated for any one of them may only be taken to a place where all of them can go.

Two people who borrowed a garment — one to wear in the morning and one in the evening — may only take it to a place where both can go. If one made an eruv toward the end of two thousand cubits to the east and the other to the west, it may not be moved from its place.

Two people who purchased an animal together and slaughtered it on Yom Tov — even if each took his portion — all the meat follows both their boundaries. But if they purchased a barrel of wine and divided it on Yom Tov, each one's portion follows his own boundary.

One who borrowed a vessel from his fellow before Yom Tov — even if he did not take it until nightfall — it follows the borrower's boundary. If he borrowed it on Yom Tov, even if he customarily borrows it every Yom Tov, it follows the lender's boundary.
A woman who borrowed water and salt from her friend for her dough and spices for her pot on Yom Tov — the dough and the cooked dish follow both their boundaries.

If one took a coal from his fellow on Yom Tov, he may only take it according to the giver's boundary. But if he lit a candle or piece of wood from his fellow's flame, it follows the boundary of the one who lit it.
A private cistern follows the boundary of its owner. One belonging to that town follows the boundary of the town's residents. One that is ownerless follows the boundary of whoever draws from it.

Flowing rivers and springing wells follow the boundary of whoever draws from them. If they flow from outside the boundary into the boundary, one may draw from them on Shabbat, and needless to say on Yom Tov.
If one drew water from an ownerless cistern for his fellow, it follows the boundary of the one who drew it.

One who had produce deposited in another town far from him — if the residents of that town made an eruv to come to him, they may not bring him his produce, since his produce follows his boundary. This applies when he designated a specific corner for them; but if he did not designate a specific corner, it follows the boundary of the one with whom it is deposited.

One who invited guests to his home on Yom Tov — they may not take portions with them to a place where the host cannot go, unless he transferred ownership of those portions to them before Yom Tov through another person.

When one comes to measure the 2000 amot teḥum of a city, if the city was long and narrow, or if it was square but not aligned with the square of the earth [i.e. the cardinal directions], but it has four square corners, we leave the size of the city as it is and measure 2000 amot in every direction from its four sides.

If the city was round, we make corners for it and view it as if it was inscribed in a rectangle, and measure 2000 amot in every direction from the sides of the rectangle. It is thus found that the corners [of the circumscribed rectangle] increase the size of the city. So too, if the city was triangular or if it had many sides, we circumscribe a rectangle around it and afterwards extend 2000 amot in every direction from outside the rectangle.

When one circumscribes a rectangle [around a city], one circumscribes it according to the cardinal directions, so that each of its sides extends according to one of the cardinal directions and is parallel to it.

If a city was wide on one end and narrow on another end, we view it as if it was entirely the maximal width. If it was shaped like the letter gamma (Γ) or like an archer's bow, if there were less than 4000 amot between the tips of the arc, we measure the teḥum from the chord of the arc and view it as if all the space between the chord and arc were full of houses. If there were [at least] 4000 amot between the tips of the arc, we measure the teḥum only from the arc itself. Rema: Some say that [in this case where the tips of the arc are at least 4000 amot apart] we measure the teḥum from the place at which the chord would be less than 4000 amot long. This is only when there is at least 2000 amot between the apex of the arc and the chord, however if there is less than 2000 amot, we measure in any case from the chord, and it is acceptable to be lenient (Hagahot Maimoniot chapter 25 from the laws of Shabbat, and the Rosh and the Tur).

Every apartment that is located outside the city, if there is a distance of 70 and two-thirds cubits between it and the city, which is equivalent to the diagonal of a side of 50 square cubits (Beit sasaim) or less, then it is considered part of the city, and when measuring the city's boundaries, it is included, except for this apartment. Rema: Some say that one should not start measuring immediately from the apartment, but rather stretch a string across the width of the city opposite the apartment and move it seventy cubits and two-thirds away from there, and start measuring from that point. This is done in every place where measuring is done (Tur). This is my opinion to be lenient.

A house that is close to a city within 70 amot (cubits), and a second house is close to the first house within 70 amot, and a third house is close to the second house within 70 amot, and so on for however many days' travel, all of them are considered as one city. And when measuring, one measures from outside the last house, provided that this house is a minimum of four cubits wide, or more. Similarly, a synagogue that has an apartment for the cantor, or a bathhouse that has an apartment for the attendant, or a treasury that has an apartment, and a bridge or a grave that has an apartment, and three walls that do not have a ceiling above them and have overlapping spaces, and also a house built in the sea, and two walls that have a ceiling above them, and a tower or a cave, all of these are considered as part of the city if they are within 70 amot and a bit from the last house. From this last house, it appears as if a thread is stretched across the entire city, and measuring is done outside of that thread at a distance of 2,000 amot in every direction except for that house. Rema: If there are two such houses opposite the city, they are considered as a city that is built like an arch. (Tur) However, two walls that do not have a ceiling above them, even if they are adjacent, and a bridge or a grave, and a synagogue or a bathhouse or a treasury that do not have an apartment, and a well, and a bush, and a cave, and a dovecote that is in a ship, and the like, are not considered as part of the city.

There were two towns, one adjacent to the other, with a distance of one hundred and thirty-one cubits between them, so that there were sixty-one and a half cubits to one town and seventy-one and a half cubits to the other town: They are considered as one city, and each one is considered as extending the entire other city, except for a distance of two thousand cubits outside the last house of each town. RAMA: If there were two houses like this facing each other, their law is like that of a city made like an arch. However, two walls without a roof between them, even if they are close to each other up to one hundred and thirty-one cubits, are considered like an enclosed area. (Tur). But a single house, even if it is very large, does not have the status of a city, and it cannot be given a distance of seventy-one and a half cubits. (Tosafot and Rosh in Chapter "Keitzad Ma'avrin" and Tur)

There were three triangular villages, if there is a distance of 1,000 cubits or less between the middle one and each of the outer ones, and between the two outer villages, the distance is less than 3,000 cubits (excluding the width of the middle village) (Tur) , in order that each one of them, together with the middle one, appears as a 2,000-cubit square. Therefore, the three villages are considered as one city-state, and a 2,000-cubit measurement is taken for each direction outside the three villages (although some say that the measurement is taken only from their walls and not from the middle one). (Tosafot, Rosh in Chapter "Keitzad Ma'avrin" and Tur)

A city that sits on the bank of a river that is dry most of the time, and people use it only when it is filled with water during rainy season: If there is a platform of four cubits width on the bank of the river, people can stand on it and use the river. The river is considered part of the city, and it is measured two thousand cubits from the second bank of the river. The entire river is considered part of the city because of the platform built on its side. If there is no platform, only the area of the houses adjacent to the river is measured, and the river is measured from the thousands of cubits of theirs.

Those who dwell in huts, meaning those who dwell in tents made of wood and reeds, do not have the law of a city. Therefore, they are not measured in thousands of cubits from the outskirts of the city, but rather from the threshold of their tents. (However, if they have a kind of enclosure of a wall or ditch that is ten cubits high around their homes). ( Beis Yosef in the name of the Shibulei Leket) If they have three courtyards of two houses each, made of stones or beams, they are all considered permanent structures, and they are measured like any other city, with a city boundary of a thousand cubits in every direction.
If a city was surrounded by a wall and then it was inbaited, its measurement is taken from the place where its settlement was located, and afterwards its wall is measured.

** With What Are the Shabbos Limits Measured; the Measurement of [Different Types of] Places; Who May Perform the Measurement. Containing 11 paragraphs** The city's boundary is only measured with a linen rope of fifty cubits, no less, because it will be too stretchable, and no longer because then it will not stretch properly
If there is a river in front of him, he measures fifty cubits until its end, and then goes back behind it by twenty-five cubits so that the span will be a complete fifty cubits until the river.
He should place the rope opposite his heart and stretch it with all his might.

A measurement should only be taken opposite the city, even if there are mountains and valleys in front of it. One should not go from beside it in a straight line and measure there, but rather measure opposite the city. When he reaches a hill, if the incline is so steep that if a plumb line were lowered from the top [of the incline], it would descend in a relatively straight line and would not diverge on an incline at the lower end of the hill for a distance of four cubits, it is not necessary to measure the ascending or descending slope [of the hill] at all. If the hill has a flat area at its top, he does not measure at all. If the plumbline moves away from being opposite him by four cubits and then contracts by ten out of fifty, meaning that in a walk of five cubits of incline, ten handbreadths rise, then he can see if the edge of the rope reaches his lip, but if it cannot be spanned by a rope of fifty cubits, he measures with a rope of four cubits. One person stands at the foot of the mountain and one above it at a distance of four cubits, and the lower one gives the rope opposite his heart and the upper one opposite his feet, and the lower one ascends to where the upper one stands and the upper one ascends four cubits, and they measure as before. If he is more inclined, for every four cubits of incline, ten handbreadths rise, so they give up on him and estimate the distance based on their judgment. If it is only fifty cubits, they estimate how much it is based on their judgment, and if it is more than fifty cubits, they measure with a rope of four cubits.

If he reaches a valley, if the plumbline diverges away from him down four cubits, one should see if it can be spanned in a rope of nine cubits from its spanning point. If not, it is measured in a rope of four cubits, and it should not be deeper than two thousand cubits. However, if it is deeper than two thousand cubits, the descent and ascent of the entire slope are measured. If the plumbline does not move away from him by four cubits, it can be spanned in a rope of nine cubits from its starting point. If not, the slope of the descent and ascent is not measured at all, but only the plain of the bottom, even if it is deeper than two thousand cubits.

If one arrives at a hill (or valley) and the entire portion of the hill or valley that is opposite the town is more than 50 cubits wide and thus it cannot be spanned, for example, [the hill or the valley] is [situated] to the east of the town, and [the person measuring] is not able to span [the hill or valley] along the entire length of that side, if [the person] can span [that distance] by proceeding within the 2000 [cubits of the Shabbos limits] to the north or to the south, he should proceed there and span [the hill or the valley], as long as it is still within the boundary of the city. If, however, [the person] cannot span [the hill or the valley] within 2000 [cubits] on the town’s sides, he should not proceed further [away from the town] to span that area.
One may rely only on a measurement made by an expert who is knowledgeable regarding the measurement of land

[The following laws apply when] the Shabbos limits [of a town] had been established and an expert came and measured [them again], maintaining that [the Shabbos limits] should be increased [in one place] and decreased [in another]: His rulings should be accepted even regarding the limits he increased. Rema: If [the expert] measured and found that the measure in the northeast [corner] is larger than the parallel measure in the southeast [corner], he should extend the line of the Shabbos limits from [the northeast corner] to the [southeast corner] on a diagonal (Rosh and the Tur). And there are those who say, the resolution or decision will be made based on the level or flatness of the location where the argument occurred. (Beis Yosef in the name of Rashi and the Rashba).

If two experts came and measured [a town’s] Shabbos limits, one [arriving at] a larger measure and the other [arriving at] a smaller one, we [accept the ruling of] the one who arrived at the larger measure. [The above applies] provided that [the larger measure] does not exceed [the smaller measure by] more than [the difference between the measuring along a diagonal from the corner of the town [and measuring from the perimeter of the town]. What is implied? It can be said that the larger measure was arrived at [for the following reason]: Perhaps the first [expert] measured the 2000 [cubits] diagonally from one corner of the city, [proceeding outward] along the diagonal, and he did the same [when measuring] from the other corner. Therefore, when a [measuring] rope is extended from the end of the Shabbos limits from one corner to the end of those limits [measured] from the other corner, the distance between this line and the city will be less than 2000 [cubits]. The [second expert, however,] measured properly, [i.e., perpendicularly] from the [border] of the city. We do not presume that the first [expert] erred by more than this amount. { Ed. Note: Therefore, if the second [expert] added a greater distance than this, [his ruling is not heeded }

The Shabbos limits around a city are configured like a square tablet, i.e., 2000 cubits are measured outward along the entire length of the eastern side of the city and the same is done on its northern side. Afterwards, it is viewed as a square tablet [measuring] 2000 [cubits] by 2000 [cubits] to fill up the corners. Thus, the corner of the Shabbos limits of 2000 cubits on a diagonal will be 2800 [cubits distant from the city]. The same pattern should be followed for all the other corners. However, one should not measure 2000 cubits [outward] diagonally from the center of one corner and do the same from the opposite corner, and then extend a [measuring] rope from one to the other. [The rationale is that] were [the person taking the measurements] to do so, he would forfeit 800 [cubits] on the diagonal, and moreover, the Shabbos limits from the [edge of the] city would be 1428 [cubits].

Even a Canaanite bondman or maidservant {who accepted the observance of the mitzvos in which women are obligated} is [considered as] trustworthy when [he or she] says: “The Shabbos limits extend until here.” A minor, by contrast, is not considered as trustworthy [regarding this matter]. Nevertheless, an adult is considered as trustworthy [if] he says, “I remember that when I was a child we would proceed until this point on Shabbos.” His testimony is relied upon.

1. ** A Traveler Who Sat Down to Rest Without Knowing Whether or Not He is Within the Shabbos Limits:** One who was on his way to enter a city and sat down on the way to rest, and darkness fell upon him and he did not realize that he was within the city limits, and later found himself within its limits, acquires a residence in the city and may traverse its entire length and breadth on Shabbat and proceed another 2000 cubits beyond the town in all directions. However, if he had absolutely no intention to enter this town and acquired a residence there instead, {i.e. the place in which he was located at the onset of Shabbos is established as his Shabbos place.} he may traverse a distance of two thousand cubits in any direction from his residence. If the 2000 [cubits] from his Shabbos place conclude in the middle of the town, he may not walk in the city beyond that point. Rema: The same law applies if he had intended to enter the city and said, "My residence is in my place," as well. (The Magid, Chapter 27)

**A Person who was Sleeping while on a Journey [when the Shabbos Commenced] is Granted 2000 Cubits in All Directions [from the Place where He was Located]:** One who sleeps on the way and darkness falls upon him, acquires a residence in his place and may traverse a distance of two thousand cubits in any direction. Specifically with regard to a person, because since if he had been awake, he would have acquired a place to sleep, he also acquires it while sleeping. However, ownerless objects do not acquire a residence, and they are like the legs of the first person to take them, who may take them to wherever he goes. However, objects belonging to non-Jews acquire a residence in their place, even though their owners are not considered residents. This ruling was made as a decree for non-Jewish objects, but Jewish objects are not subject to such a decree. And those who bring them [objects] into a city may move them within the entire city, which is like an area of four cubits, provided that the city is surrounded for dwelling purposes. Small, walled towns are considered to be surrounded for dwelling purposes, even if the houses were built first and the walls were erected around them later. However, simple fortresses are not considered to be surrounded for dwelling purposes. Rema: Therefore, Jews should be careful not to lend their objects to non-Jews and have them returned on Shabbat to be moved more than four cubits, unless the city is surrounded by a wall for dwelling purposes. This is because the objects acquire a residence in the non-Jewish domain.

**The Laws that Apply to a Trench Filled with Water Located Between the Shabbos Limits of Two Towns:** When water collected within a trench located between the Shabbos limits of two towns, and filled it, with part of [the trench] located in the Shabbos limits of one town and part in the Shabbos limits of the other, [the residents of] both towns are forbidden to draw [water] from it [on Shabbos], even though [the residents of] each [town] are drawing water from within their own Shabbos limits. [The rationale is that] the residents within a techum (Sabbath limit) acquire ownership of the city, and these residents can intermingle with each other. However, it is necessary to make a partition at the end of the boundaries to separate them. Even if the partition is suspended and does not touch the ground of the ditch, it is still valid. As for the ownership of the non-permanent structures, it is considered insignificant. Rema: And a pit of straw standing between these two domains, those eat from here and these eat from here, and there is no concern that one will take from the portion of his fellow. (Chulin) And if the water is drawn, no correction is needed, as they do not acquire a dwelling and they are like the feet that fill [the space].

**The Laws Applying to a Group of Fields that Non-Jews Enclosed [on Shabbos],** [The following laws apply when a person] spent Shabbos in a group of fields and non-Jews enclosed [the area] on Shabbos with partitions erected for the purpose of habitation One may only carry an object in a public domain that is not completely enclosed by walls, roofs, and partitions up to a distance of four cubits, unless an eruv has been established. It is permitted to [transfer articles] within the entire [enclosure, if the person does so] by throwing [the article], for [the person] may throw an article even beyond the 2000 [cubits comprising his Shabbos limits]. It is considered as if it is surrounded by a wall for the purposes of carrying inside it on Shabbat But to carry something beyond four cubits is prohibited, even within two thousand cubits (Beit Yosef citing Tosafot and Hagahot Ashri, chapter of "Mi She'hutziah").

**The laws governing whether the Shabbos limits applies ten hand breadths above [the Ground]:** Concerning a person who walks more than 1o Tefachim outside the domain, such as jumping on top of ten-foot tall columns, and each one of them does not have a measurement of four hand breadths by four hand breadths, thus it is doubtful whether there are any areas above ten hand breadths or not. And when it is a Rabbinic law, its doubt will be resolved leniently. Rema: However, if one was walking on this path or by jumping there from within twelve cubits outside of twelve cubits, we follow the more stringent opinion, which states that the boundaries are twelve cubits according to Torah law (see my own words and Responsa of the Rambam). All authorities agree that the Scriptural prohibition [against going beyond] the Shabbos limits does not apply [to travel] on seas and rivers even [when one goes] beyond twelve mil, because do not resemble the encampment in the desert. When a person is traveling in a ship on Shabbos and arrives at a harbor [on that day], if [the ship] was always traveling ten handbreadths above seabed or riverbed from the commencement of the Shabbos until [the time when] the ship reached the harbor, [the person] is not considered [as one who] went beyond his Shabbos limits, and this person has 200o cubits from the place where he was lower than 10 tefachim. Rema: But if there is doubt whether it is above ten handbreadths or not, we follow the lenient opinion (see Ha-Maggid, Ch. 27). But if he has already gone two thousand cubits from the point where he landed downwards, he only has four cubits [of space to move] nevertheless, if he needs to leave the boat due to rain falling on him, or because the sun is shining on him, or because he needs to relieve himself, and because of these strong burdens he needs this [leniency] to enter the city, then he has the entire city as his four cubits. (this is the opinion of Al-Ashari, Mordechai, and the glosses of Asheri on Chapter "Mi She-Hotzi'o" [of the Talmudic tractate Shabbat]. See later in Siman Tav-Vav (516) and see earlier in Siman Resh-Samech-Vav (246) regarding one who is riding on the road and darkness falls upon him on Erev Shabbat, what should he do.

**Laws of those who leave the Techum** One who leaves the Shabbat barrier even a single amah (cubit), he should not enter to be like a member of the city, and he only has four amot from [where] he is standing and out.
If his leg is inside the barrier and one leg is outside the barrier, he should enter.

One, when Shabbat begins, is outside the barrier of the city, even a single amah, he should not enter to be like a member of the city, and he should only walk two thousand amot in each direction from the place he was in when Shabbat began.

One who leaves the barrier without knowing, it is permitted to make a divider for himself of what people made an eruv with, in that direction and they are able to walk there. And they will make around him like a divider and he will enter between them. And the one who does not know the ones who made their dividers that are called like this, but if he left knowingly, it is prohibited.

The one that was taken out of the Shabbat barrier by non-Jews or a bad spirit or other unwilling [removals] or by accident, and he left, he only has four amot. They return him within the barrier, it is like he did not leave, and the whole city is like four amot like at first, and beyond that two thousand amot in every direction. But, if he returns knowingly, he only has four amot. Gloss: And if he entered a boat and the boat went out of the barrier, and returned afterwards to the port that it departed from, it is like he did not leave, because it is considered like non-Jews took him out and returned him (Or Zarua).

Non-Jews place him outside of the Shabbat barrier in an enclosure, in a prison, or in a cave, or in a different city surrounded by a wall as a dwelling, or he was forced the rest of the types of forced circumstances, or it was an accident and he went out of the barrier and entered into one of those, and then he remembered and he was inside, he can walk in all of it; but if he went out of the barrier knowingly, even though it was one of these, he only has four amot.

The one that departed on his boat in the sea, he can walk all of it since he stopped in the "air" of the dividers; and if the walls of the boat were opened on Shabbat, if it went, he can walk all of it, if it stands, he can only walk four amot. Gloss: And if in the middle, he has ten walls and he does not have anything on his head, we go after the middle, and even if he does not have anything other than to draw a limit of ten, that we say, we limit to complete (Or Zarua).

He if went out knowingly and returned by way of non-Jews, he only has four amot; however, if he went out of the city walled for dwelling (The Rosh chapter One who went out and Rabbi Yerucham HY''H and Or Zarua) all of it is like four amot; and even if he went out knowingly and returned knowingly. Look later of the laws of cities Siman 401.

Fruit that was taken out of the Shabbat barrier and returned, they do not lose their place as the whole city is for them like four amot and two thousand amot further in every direction like from the outset if it is a Yom Tov; And if it is Shabbat, it is permitted regarding eating in their place, and even for the same Jew that returned them for his need intentionally, 49, they are forced circumstances. And the whole time that they are not returned and they are outside their place, if he took them out accidentally, it is permitted to eat them, but it is prohibited to move them out to eat them for four amot, and if he took them out intentionally it is prohibited to eat them even one who did not take them out. And there are those who permit for the one who did not take them out.

One who went out of the Shabbat barrier unknowingly, he only has four amot, and if he needs to "go do the bathroom", he is able to leave from there until he finds a private place to turn; and it is good advice that he approaches the side of the barrier, because if he does not find a private place until the barrier he can enter, and after he enters, it is like he did not leave since he entered with permission; but if he found a private place first, he should not enter except to face there, and he should distance himself from the place he turned until he covers the smell, and there he has four amot. And if he distances himself from the smell and enters into the barrier, it is like he did not leave. And if he went out knowingly, he has no fix. This that we said, regarding the need to "go to the bathroom", there are those who say even for urine and there are those who say specifically for feces.

One who went out of the Shabbat barrier with permission, for example a midwife brought a child or things like that, she has two thousand amot in each direction from that spot that he arrived at; and if he arrived to a city, then he is like the people of the city and he has two thousand [amot] in each direction outside the city (look at the end of Siman 248.)

If he goes out with permission and walks on the path, and they said to him: the mitzvah is already made when you went out to do [it], he has from his place two thousand amot in each direction; if he has a little of the barrier that he went out from with permission, it is absorbed within the two thousand amot that he has from his place, when he returns to his place it is like he didn't go out.

All those who venture forth to rescue from the hands of non-Jews, or from the river, or from the rubble – have two thousand cubits in each direction from the place of rescue; and if the hand of the non-Jews was powerful, and [the rescuers] were afraid to remain in the place of rescue, they may return on Shabbat to their own location, with their weapons.

**Laws of placing an eruv and acquiring Shabbat rest. Contains 4 sections** (It is permitted to make an eruv of boundaries and acquire Shabbat rest at the end of the boundary, and therefore:) One who left the city on Shabbat eve and placed two meals' worth of food at a distance from the city within the boundary and established his Shabbat rest there — even if he returned to the city and slept in his house — he is considered as if he spent Shabbat at the place where he placed the two meals. This is called an eruv of boundaries. He may walk from the place of his eruv the next day two thousand cubits in each direction. Therefore when he walks from his eruv two thousand cubits in the direction of the city, he may only walk within the city until the end of his measure. If the city is contained within his measure, the entire city counts as four cubits and he completes his measure beyond it. How so? If he placed his eruv one thousand cubits east of his house in the city, he may walk two thousand cubits east from his eruv, and two thousand cubits west from his eruv — one thousand from the eruv to his house and one thousand cubits from his house within the city — and he may only walk within the city until the end of that thousand. If from his house to the end of the city is less than a thousand — even by one cubit — so that his measure ends beyond the city, the entire city counts as four cubits and he may walk 996 cubits beyond it to complete the two thousand. Therefore if he placed his eruv two thousand cubits from his house in the city, he has lost the entire city and may walk from his house to the eruv two thousand cubits, but may not walk even one cubit from his house into the city in the western direction. Rema: Some say that even if his measure ends in the middle of the city he may walk through the entire city but not beyond it, and one may be lenient. And if his measure ends at the edge of the city, even though there is still an extension beyond the city, the entire city counts as four cubits — we do not say the city's extension counts as the city to be stringent. Wherever one places an eruv of boundaries and has two thousand cubits in each direction, he is only permitted to walk north and south within the width of the place where he acquired Shabbat rest. If it is only four cubits — such as when the eruv is not in a private domain — he may only walk in each direction two thousand cubits within the width of his four cubits and their corners, as explained above in Siman 398, section 2. Nevertheless, if his measure ends at the edge of the city and the entire city counts as his four cubits, he may walk its entire width and has two thousand cubits beyond the city to the north and south, even if he does not have that width opposite the place where he acquired the eruv.

One who places his eruv in a private domain — even if it were a large city like Nineveh, or even a ruined city or a cave fit for dwelling — may walk through all of it and two thousand cubits beyond it in each direction.

One who places his eruv within the city where he spent Shabbat has accomplished nothing, and we do not measure from the place of his eruv — rather he is like all the city's residents who have two thousand cubits in each direction beyond the city. Similarly, if he placed his eruv in places that combine with the city from whose edge the boundary is measured, it is as if he placed it within the city.
If he placed his eruv beyond the boundary it is ineffective. (And he has his boundary measured from his house.)

**Laws of where the eruv is placed. Contains 13 sections** One who places his eruv in a cemetery — it is not a valid eruv, since a cemetery is forbidden in benefit, and since he wants the eruv to remain there after acquisition he is thereby benefiting from it. If he placed it in a beit hapras, it is a valid eruv, even for a priest, since he can enter there in a sealed chest or by blowing the ground as he walks.

The person and his eruv must be in the same domain so that it is possible for him to eat it during twilight. Therefore if he intended to spend Shabbat in a public domain and placed his eruv in a private domain, or intended to spend Shabbat in a private domain and placed his eruv in a public domain — it is not a valid eruv, since he cannot carry from a private domain to a public domain during twilight except through a transgression. But if he intended to spend Shabbat in a private domain or public domain and placed his eruv in a karmelit, or intended to spend Shabbat in a karmelit and placed his eruv in a private domain or public domain — it is a valid eruv, since during twilight when the eruv is acquired it is permitted to carry between either of those two domains and a karmelit for a matter of mitzva, as anything rabbinic was not decreed upon during twilight in a case of mitzva or pressing need.

If he placed it on top of a reed or giant reed growing from the ground — it is not a valid eruv, since being soft and easy to snap would make one liable for a sin-offering, and they decreed regarding them (and if they are as soft as a vegetable, see above at the beginning of Siman 336) even during twilight and even in a case of mitzva. If they were detached and stuck into the ground, it is a valid eruv.
If he placed it in a tower and locked it and the key was lost before Shabbat, or a rockslide fell upon it — if he can retrieve it without performing a biblically prohibited labor, it is a valid eruv.

Whoever places his eruv in a place has four cubits at the place of his eruv. Therefore one who places his eruv of boundaries at the end of his boundary and it rolled within four cubits — it is a valid eruv. If it rolled beyond four cubits, it is not a valid eruv.

If his eruv was lost, burned, or if it was at the end of the boundary and rolled beyond four cubits, or if it was terumah and became impure before nightfall — it is not a valid eruv. If it happened after nightfall — it is a valid eruv, since eruv acquisition occurs at twilight. If there is doubt, it is valid, as a doubtful eruv is valid — provided it had a presumption of validity, such as this case where he placed it there and a doubt arose. But if it had no presumption of validity — such as doubt whether it was placed there at all — no.

How is an eruv made? If one wishes to go to the end of the boundary or within it and let nightfall find him there — this is the primary way of fulfilling the mitzva. Even if he did not say "my Shabbat rest is in my place" but simply let nightfall find him there and said nothing — whether one who goes out from his house to let nightfall find him at the boundary, or one who was traveling and nightfall came upon him — he acquires two thousand cubits without any declaration. If he does not wish to trouble himself to be there at nightfall, he may go while it is still day and place there two meals' worth of food — each person according to his food requirement; if he is ill or a large eater, the measure is two average meals which is six eggs' worth of bread (see above Siman 368, section 3, or any food used for partnership of alleyways) — and if it is a relish, enough to eat with it two meals suffices. He then says "through this eruv I will be permitted to walk two thousand cubits tomorrow," and returns and sleeps in his house. Even so, his boundary is measured from the place of his eruv, since we consider him as if he lives there. But students who eat by householders whose homes are in the field and return to sleep in their teacher's house — their boundary is measured from their teacher's house, which is their sleeping place and their primary location, since that is where they would want to eat as well if their food were there.

If he wishes, he may send the eruv through an agent and say "through this eruv so-and-so shall be permitted to walk" — provided the agent is not deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, or one who does not believe in the eruv. If he sent it through a deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, non-Jew, or one who does not believe in the eruv — it is not a valid eruv. But if he told another to receive it from the agent and sent it through one of these — even if he sent it by elephant or monkey and saw from a distance that it arrived and was given to the receiver — it is a valid eruv, even if he did not see the other person place it, since we presume an agent carries out his mission. Similarly, many who made a partnership eruv of boundaries and wished to send their eruv through another may do so.

If one person or many said to someone "go and make an eruv for us" and he made it for them in whichever direction he chose — it is a valid eruv and they may use it, since they did not specify a direction for him.

If one said to his fellow "make an eruv for me with dates" and he made it with dried figs; with dried figs and he made it with dates; "place my eruv in the tower" and he placed it in the dovecote; "in the dovecote" and he placed it in the tower; "in the house" and he placed it in the upper story; "in the upper story" and he placed it in the house — it is not a valid eruv. But if he said "make an eruv for me" without specification and he made it — whether with dried figs or dates, whether in the house or upper story — it is a valid eruv.

One who was traveling and recognized a tree or fence at the end of two thousand cubits and feared nightfall might come before he arrived there, and said "my Shabbat rest is beneath it at its base" — he acquires Shabbat rest at its base and has two thousand cubits from there, even if he cannot reach there before nightfall at a normal walking pace unless he runs. He is permitted to go there at a normal pace even if he does not arrive before nightfall. But if he could not reach there at all before nightfall, he may not move from his place, since he uprooted his intention from here and did not acquire there either. This applies specifically when he specified four cubits that are within two thousand cubits — such as saying "my Shabbat rest is at its base" and the distance from here to its base is no more than two thousand. But if the entire tree is not within two thousand cubits and he did not specify a place beneath it, he has not acquired Shabbat rest — since perhaps he had in mind four cubits that are beyond two thousand — and here too he has not acquired, since he uprooted his intention from here, and he may not move from his place. If the entire tree stands within two thousand cubits and he did not specify his Shabbat rest location — such as saying "my Shabbat rest is beneath it" — he has four thousand cubits from his location toward the tree, minus the measure of the tree's spread beneath it; for example if the tree's spread is twenty cubits, he has two thousand minus twenty cubits there. According to Rambam, one who acquires Shabbat rest at a distant place without specifying his Shabbat rest location has not acquired Shabbat rest there but only at the place where he was standing when nightfall came. Similarly if he said "my Shabbat rest is in such-and-such place" and it is more than two thousand cubits away, he acquires Shabbat rest at his own location. One who says "my Shabbat rest is beneath such-and-such tree" — if the area beneath it is eight cubits or more, he has not acquired Shabbat rest since he did not specify his Shabbat rest location; therefore he must intend to rest at its base or within four cubits to its north or south. If the area beneath it is less than eight cubits and he intended to rest beneath it, he has acquired Shabbat rest since his location is at least partially specified. The Rif rules similarly.

If there were two people, one who recognizes the place and one who does not — the one who does not recognize it entrusts his Shabbat rest to the one who does and says "our Shabbat rest is in such-and-such place."
This leniency was permitted only for a traveler, but not for one who is at home. If he said so, it does not count for him and he has only the Shabbat rest of his home.

**Laws of one who sets out on the road to acquire Shabbat rest. Contains 3 sections** One who intended to establish his Shabbat rest at a place known to him and set out on the road walking toward that place in order to reach it and acquire Shabbat rest there — even if he did not arrive and did not stand there, but his fellow turned him back to sleep, or he himself turned back to sleep by him, or he was delayed — he may walk the next day to the place he intended, and from that place two thousand cubits in each direction. Since he resolved in his mind to establish his Shabbat rest there and set out on the road, he is considered as if he had stood there or placed his eruv there. This applies to a poor person whom we do not trouble to place an eruv, or to one who was far away such as a traveler. But if he was neither poor nor far away — no.

What we said about one who acquires Shabbat rest at a distant place by setting out on the road — he need not go out and walk into a field; even if he descended from an upper story to go to that place and before he left the courtyard gate his fellow turned him back — he has set out and acquired Shabbat rest. And anyone who acquires Shabbat rest at a distant place need not say "my Shabbat rest is in such-and-such place" — once he resolved in his mind and set out on the road even a little he has acquired Shabbat rest there. Needless to say, one who went on foot and stood at the place where he acquires Shabbat rest need not say anything at all — once he resolved in his mind he has acquired.

Townspeople who sent one of their number to bring their eruv to a known place, and he set out on the road and his fellow turned him back and he did not bring their eruv — they have not acquired Shabbat rest at that place since their eruv was not placed there, and they may only walk two thousand cubits in each direction within their town. But he has acquired Shabbat rest there, since he was traveling and intended to rest there and set out on the road. Therefore he may walk to that place the next day and walk from it two thousand cubits in each direction.

**One whose home is in the east and he placed the eruv in the west. Contains 1 section** One who is in the east with his home in the field, and told his agent to make an eruv for him in the west — if the agent placed the eruv beyond his home such that it is more than two thousand cubits from him and his home is closer to him within two thousand cubits, the eruv is void and he retains the Shabbat rest of his home. If the agent placed the eruv such that it is within two thousand cubits of him — even though his home is also within two thousand cubits of him — he acquires Shabbat rest at the place of his eruv and not at his home.

**Laws of one who divides his eruv. Contains one section** One who made an eruv for the first half of the day toward the north and the second half toward the south — thinking mistakenly that this is possible — or one who said to two people "make an eruv for me" and one made it for him toward the north and one toward the south: if each placed his eruv at the end of two thousand cubits, he may not move from his place since it is unknown which eruv took effect for him. If the eruvs were not placed at the end of two thousand cubits, he may walk as far as possible by virtue of both of them. How so? If each placed his eruv at the end of one thousand cubits from his home, he has one thousand cubits from his home toward each of the eruvs. If one placed his eruv to the east at the end of one thousand cubits and the other placed his to the west at the end of five hundred cubits, he may walk one thousand cubits to the west by virtue of what the eastern eruv left him, and one thousand five hundred cubits to the east by virtue of what the western eruv left him.

**Laws of one who makes an eruv for many. Contains one section** One who makes an eruv for many from his own food says "this eruv is for all the townspeople, and whoever wishes may rely on it" — provided it contains two meals' worth for each person. He must transfer ownership to them through another suitable person, as with eruv of courtyards (see above Siman 366, section 10) , and he must inform them. Whoever he informed before Shabbat — even if that person did not resolve in his mind to rely on it while it was still day but only after nightfall — it is a valid eruv. But if he did not inform him before Shabbat, he cannot rely on it after nightfall. Similarly, one who placed an eruv for all the Shabbatot of the year and said "whichever one I choose I will go and rely on it" — even if he did not resolve in his mind until the next day, he may rely on it. Similarly, one who heard that a scholar was coming and did not know from which direction, and placed two eruvs and said "whichever direction the scholar comes from, that eruv shall take effect for me" — the eruv in the direction the scholar came from takes effect. Or if he said "if he does not come at all I will be like the townspeople," or "if two scholars come I will go wherever I wish" — everything follows his condition. Similarly, if he said to two or three people "I hereby make an eruv for whichever of you I choose" — even if he did not specify whom he chose until nightfall, it is a valid eruv.

**That one may only make an eruv with someone's knowledge. Contains 2 sections** One may not make an eruv of boundaries for a person without his knowledge, since perhaps he does not wish to make an eruv in the direction this one chose — except for his minor son and daughter even if they do not eat at his table, and his Canaanite manservant and maidservant, even if they protested against making the eruv for them and even if they made another eruv themselves, it is void. But for his adult son and daughter even if they eat at his table, his Hebrew manservant and maidservant, and his wife — he may only make an eruv with their knowledge. If he made an eruv for them and they heard and were silent and did not protest, they may use his eruv. But if they protested or made another eruv for themselves, his eruv is not valid for them.
A child of six years or younger goes out by virtue of his mother's eruv, and one need not place two meals' worth of food for him separately.

**That one may only make an eruv of boundaries for a matter of mitzva. Contains 4 sections** One may only make an eruv of boundaries for a matter of mitzva — such as wishing to go to a house of mourning, or to a wedding feast, or to greet his teacher or friend who came from a journey, and similar cases. Rema: Or if he wishes to go for a stroll on Yom Tov or Shabbat in an orchard, which brings joy — this is considered a matter of mitzva. Or out of fear, such as wishing to flee from non-Jews or bandits and the like, in which case he is permitted to go even for an optional matter. And if he made an eruv for none of these but for an optional matter, it is nonetheless a valid eruv.
One may not make an eruv of boundaries during twilight, but if he did make one it is valid.

If two people said to someone "go and make an eruv for us" — one made an eruv for him while it was still day and one made an eruv for him during twilight: the eruv made for him while it was still day was eaten during twilight, and the eruv made for him during twilight was eaten after nightfall — both have acquired a valid eruv. Some disagree.

When placing an eruv of boundaries one recites the blessing on the mitzva of eruv and says "through this eruv I shall be permitted to walk from such-and-such place two thousand cubits in each direction." If he is making an eruv for many he says "so-and-so and so-and-so shall be permitted" or "the residents of such-and-such place shall be permitted."

**Laws of an eruv of boundaries on a Yom Tov that falls adjacent to Shabbat. Contains 5 sections** When Yom Tov falls adjacent to Shabbat — whether before or after it — or for the two days of Yom Tov observed in the diaspora, one may make two eruvs in two directions and rely on whichever he wishes for the first day and on the eruv in the other direction for the second day. Or he may make one eruv in one direction and rely on it for one of the two days, and on the second day he is like the townspeople as if he made no eruv, having two thousand cubits in each direction. This applies to the two days of Yom Tov in the diaspora, but the two days of Rosh Hashana are considered as one day, and one may only make an eruv for both days in one direction. Similarly, one may make a condition on his eruv and say "this eruv is for this Shabbat but not for another Shabbat," "for another Shabbat but not for this one," "for Shabbatot but not for Yom Tov," "for Yom Tov but not for Shabbatot."

One who makes an eruv for two days of Yom Tov in the diaspora, or for Shabbat and Yom Tov — even if it is one eruv in one direction for both days — the eruv must be present in its place during twilight of the first night and during twilight of the second night. How does he do this? He brings it to that place on Yom Tov eve or Shabbat eve and lets nightfall find him there, then takes it in his hand and returns. If the first night is Yom Tov he brings it to that place the next day and leaves it there until nightfall and eats it if the second night is Shabbat, or brings it back if the second night is Yom Tov — since they are two separate sanctities and not one day, so that we cannot say that by acquiring the eruv on the first night it takes effect for both days. If the eruv was eaten on the first day, it took effect for the first day and is not an eruv for the second. If he acquired Shabbat rest by foot on the first day, he must acquire it by foot on the second day — by going and standing at that place and resolving in his mind to acquire Shabbat rest there, saying nothing, since it is forbidden to make any preparation from Yom Tov for Shabbat or from Shabbat for Yom Tov even by speech. Certainly he cannot make an eruv with bread that was not already used on the first day, since he would need to declare it an eruv and would thereby be making a preparation. If he made the eruv on the first day with food and wishes to acquire by foot on the second day, it is valid. If he wishes to make the eruv with bread on the second day, he must use the same bread he used on the first day, needing to say nothing since the eruv was already declared — and thus he is making no preparation at all.

What we said about making two eruvs in two directions for two days applies only when it is possible for him to reach each of the two eruvs on the first day. But if it is impossible to reach the second day's eruv on the first day, the second eruv is not valid, since the mitzva of eruv requires it to be accessible as a meal while it is still day — and since he cannot reach this eruv on the first day, it is not accessible while it is still day. How so? If he placed his eruv two thousand cubits east of his home and relied on it for the first day, and placed a second eruv one cubit, one hundred cubits, or one thousand cubits west and relied on it for the second day — the second eruv is not valid, since on the first day the second eruv is not accessible to him while it is still day, as nothing remains for him to the west. But if he placed his eruv one thousand five hundred cubits east of his home and relied on it for the first day, and placed a second eruv within five hundred cubits west of his home and relied on it for the second day — it is valid, since he can reach it on the first day.
Yom Kippur is like Shabbat regarding both eruv of courtyards and eruv of boundaries.
Yom Tov observes the eruv of boundaries but not the eruv of courtyards.

**Contains 1 paragraph:** On the beginning of the month, it is permitted to do work. However, those women who follow a custom to not engage in work [are following] a good custom. Rema: And if the custom is to do some kinds of work and not to do some [other] kinds of work, we follow the custom.
** The law of fasting on the beginning of the month. Containing five sections.** On the beginning of the month it is forbidden to fast.

Fasts are not decreed for the congregation to occur on the beginning of the month, on Chanukah, or on Purim. If they began, i.e. they declared a fast of a specified number of days, beginning from before the beginning of the month, then even on the first of the month they shall not disrupt [the fast. Instead] they shall fast and remedy it.

An individual who commits himself to a fast of a specified number of days, and the beginning of the month interrupts, or if he commits himself to fast on the beginning of the month: If he committed himself using common language of accepting fast, he does not require formal release from his vow (and his pledge is automatically abrogated). But if he committed himself with the phrasing "I hereby accept upon myself," i.e. the language used for an oath, he needs to be released from his vow by a sage. See Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 216 section 3.

If he swore to fast a specified number of days and the beginning of the month happened to be included among them, the oath is binding upon him because of the general prohibition. However, if he explicitly swore to fast on the beginning of the month, it appears to me that the oath is binding on him because the [prohibition] has only a rabbinical source. Yet from the words of Rambam, it appears that the source is biblical. See earlier, chapter 570.
One who fasts for a dream on the beginning of the month, on Chanukah, or on Purim, must add a [second] fast onto his fast.
It is a Mitzvah to feast a lot on Rosh Chodesh.

**Whether women are permitted to wail on Rosh Chodesh. Contains 2 sections** Over the dead, women may chant dirges where all say together and clap, meaning striking palm against palm, but they may not keen, where one leads and the others respond after her. After the dead is buried they may neither chant dirges nor clap.

One recites Tziduk Hadin and Kaddish. Rema: This is not the custom — see Yoreh Deah Siman 401, section 6 in the gloss. Similarly on all days when Tachanun is not recited, and similarly on Shabbat eve after midday. Some say that if one is buried at night, Kaddish and Tziduk Hadin are not recited. (Kol Bo)

**The recitation of "And on your new moons" in Pesukei Dezimra. Contains one section** The custom in Ashkenaz is to recite the passage of "And on your new moons" in the morning service after the passage of the daily offering. In Sepharad the custom is not to recite it, since it will be read later from the Torah scroll.
